To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there are four different computerised instruments for collecting time-use data in epidemiological studies; they were developed independently but had many similarities; they showed broad agreement in the time spent in sleep, MVPA and personal care; and they differed in the amount of sedentary time and LPA reported.
“Four different computerised use of time instruments were used to collect population time use data from a collective of 8,286 adults from four different population studies.
the use-of-time instruments are self-administered computerised tools that capture energy expenditure and time spent in various activities, including MVPA and sedentary time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of instruments that can provide a comprehensive assessment of time use and physical activity.
the development and validation of computerised instruments for measuring physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep.
how people use their time in different ways and how these patterns are related to health and well-being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these four instruments are all useful, but they do not capture the same things.
there is no one best way to measure physical activity in epidemiological studies.
the instruments have similar validity for physical activity, but that the differences between them are large enough to preclude their being used interchangeably in the same study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the four use-of-time instruments described in this paper have shown that it is feasible to use computerised use-of-day recalls to collect data on physical activity, sitting, and sleep.
we need to be more precise in defining and measuring physical activity, sleep, and sedentary behaviour, and to consider these in a 24-hour context, rather than in isolation.
we are not yet able to capture all the relevant behaviours and activities in a single instrument.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the four instruments described in this paper can be used in epidemiological studies to provide a comprehensive picture of physical activity and time use.
it is possible to collect high quality data on physical activity and sedentariness using computerised use-of time instruments, but that the data are not directly comparable across studies.
the use-of-time instruments can be used to provide population-level estimates of time use, but the specific activities and behaviours that are captured will depend on the instrument used.
